wstep: This card describes the NCHFP method for canning whole sweet or sour cherries in a boiling-water canner, here for sour cherries.

akapity: Stem and wash the cherries; you may remove the pits.
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml.
If you pit them, put them in water containing ascorbic acid so they do not darken at the stem end.
If you leave the pits in, prick the skins on opposite sides with a clean needle so they do not split.
Cherries may be canned in water, apple juice, white grape juice or syrup.
Syrup helps keep the flavor, color and shape of the fruit, but it does not prevent spoilage.
For a very light syrup (about 10% sugar) NCHFP uses 6 1/2 cups of water and 3/4 cup of sugar for a load of 9 pint jars, or 10 1/2 cups of water and 1 1/4 cups of sugar for 7 quart jars.
Heat the water and sugar together and bring to a boil.
Hot pack: in a large saucepan bring the drained cherries to a boil with 1/2 cup of water, juice or syrup for each quart of fruit.
Fill the jars with the cherries and cooking liquid, leaving 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace.
Raw pack: put 1/2 cup of hot water, juice or syrup into each jar and fill it with drained cherries, shaking them down gently as you fill.
Add more hot liquid, leaving 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace.
Put on the lids and process.
At 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process hot-packed pints for 15 minutes and quarts for 20, and raw-packed pints or quarts for 25 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–3000 ft (above 300 m up to 900 m): hot pack 20 minutes for pints and 25 for quarts, raw pack 30 minutes.
At 3001–6000 ft (above 900 m up to 1800 m): hot pack 20 minutes for pints and 30 for quarts, raw pack 35 minutes.
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m): hot pack 25 minutes for pints and 35 for quarts, raw pack 40 minutes.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m, 3000 ft becomes 900 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
NCHFP times are for US jar sizes: a pint holds about 473 ml and a quart about 946 ml.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): for a jar of up to 473 ml use the pint time, and for a larger jar of up to 946 ml, for example 0.5 l or 0.9 l, use the quart time.
This NCHFP recipe gives no time for jars larger than a quart, such as 1 l, so use smaller jars.
